subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT RESPONSE TO SIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 99(2), I have the honour to lay upon the table copies, in both official languages, of the Government's response to recommendations 1, 2 and 3 of the Sixth Report of the Standing Committee on Government Operations.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Hawkes (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106(8), I have the honour to table, in both official languages, the Government's response to petitions Nos. 332-4800, 332-4801, 332-4803, 3324807 and 332-4813.
[Editors Note: See todays Votes and Proceedings.]

Mr. Speaker, for some months now, Canadians from all parts of the country have expressed their serious concern about the way in which financial institutions have been imposing charges for banking services. Today I am announcing a wide ranging package of measures which will respond to these concerns.
Four principles have guided me in developing this initiative. First, free market competition is the best way to obtain and maintain fair pricing practices. Fundamental to such competition is the informed consumer. The consumer must have the information if he or she is to act intelligently.
Third, certain basic banking services should be available at little or no cost. Fourth, customers should have a clear understanding of their recourse when they have complaints about services.

Mr. Speaker, the government has decided to take strong and direct action to ensure that Canadian consumers are fairly treated when charges related to bank and trust company accounts are imposed. Canadians will now be properly informed, in advance, of charges relating to their personal accounts. We will amend the Bank Act and Canada's major banks and federally regulated trust companies will take voluntarily action with respect to basic banking services and certain objectionable charges.

In simple terms, we are achieving results which will benefit consumers. Where necessary, we are acting through statutory and regulatory improvement. Elsewhere, we are achieving these results by allowing the voluntary and market-driven business environment to operate. We have moved on all three fronts, regulatory, legislative and voluntary.
Some in this House, no doubt, would prefer that we avoid the use of legislation in answer to this problem of bank service charges. Others would prefer that we legislate all aspects of this initiative, leaving no room for voluntary action. In my view, our initiative today strikes the appropriate balance between legislated rights and obligations and voluntary action on the part of the financial institutions.
Providing Canadians with more information, while allowing financial institutions the freedom to maintain their competitive and pricing decisions, is an appropriate response to the problems identified by Canadians. In the process of identifying those problems, I want to pay tribute to the Members of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs who have worked to broaden public understanding of this problem. Their recommendations have provided the foundation for the measures being outlined here today.
I believe the way in which this issue has been examined and resolved is an excellent example of our parliamentary reform

June 30, 1988
Statements by Ministers
which was introduced by this Government. All Parties in this House, and as I look across the floor I say very clearly, all Parties in this House have worked constructively to achieve the progress which I am announcing today. I am hopeful I can count on that same constructive spirit to expedite the passage of the legislation.
Let me deal with the statutory changes to the Bank Act being brought forward today. New legislative requirements make full disclosure of commonly applied charges a fundamental part of this plan. The legislation will also ensure that customers are fully informed of service charges and the complaints procedure when opening a personal account.

Furthermore, our legislation will ensure that any increases in charges, or any new charges, cannot be imposed until there is proper notification. This will be achieved by distribution of a notice with statements, where applicable, and through prominent posting in all bank branches across Canada.
Moreover, posting will be required not only in branches, Mr. Speaker, but also at automated banking machines.

The statutory and regulatory changes are not only consistent with the recommendations of the Finance Committee but go somewhat further to ensure that customers are made fully aware of all account related service charges. I am today tabling the background material after this statement which provides a full description of the new disclosure requirements in the amended Bank Act and regulations. I believe that major federal trust companies will bring their disclosure practices in line with these provisions as well.
There is a fundamental principle which our initiative entrenches-no financial institution ought to alter its charges without its customers being fully informed in advance. This must be done. Consumers have the right to be able to make informed choices among available account options.
Following discussions between the Government and the financial institutions I am pleased to announce today that the major Canadian banks and the major Canadian trust companies will continue to provide, and in many cases enhance, their basic accounts. As a result of all this, most of the major federal deposit-taking institutions-the preponderance of them-will give their customers access to basic accounts, which will do what? They will allow unlimited deposits and unlimited cash withdrawals without charges, without maintenance fees and without minimum balance requirements. It can now be said as a result of this that all Canadians, economically disadvantaged Canadians especially, have or very soon will have access to basic banking services at little or no cost.
We shall be monitoring carefully compliance with these actions. We hope this voluntary action will be sufficient. But I emphasize that the Government will not hesitate to take
legislative steps in the future should that prove necessary. We have it voluntarily now and we will act in the future if the voluntary system breaks down.
In order to assist consumers in making informed decisions about the cost and type of banking services to which they can have access, my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), has agreed to publish a comparison table outlining available basic banking services, together with their costs. This will also help to ensure that the public can monitor financial institutions' compliance.
Let me move to certain reprehensible and objectionable charges referred to by the House committee. These charges have been or will be withdrawn. The results are as follows. I invite the House to listen carefully to these charges that will be withdrawn. First, recipients of NSF cheques will not be charged for depositing these cheques in their personal accounts. Second, there will be no charge for closing personal accounts which have been open for more than 90 days.

Third, there will not be charges for the maintenance of an institution basic account when the balance falls below a specified minimum level. Fourth, there will be no charge for any transactions resulting from an institution's error. Finally, administration and transfer fees on fixed-term deposits, notes and GICs will not be increased during the term of the instrument. Where necessary, this will be noted in the contract.

I am also pleased to announce that we will be taking specific measures to strengthen the process of handling consumer complaints concerning bank and trust company service charges. I discussed this problem with the major banks and with trust companies, that is, the need to enhance their complaint resolution procedures. This morning I went in to see my own branch manager in Ottawa. I asked him what his procedures were. He outlined that they varied from branch to branch and from bank to bank. He would welcome clarification and standardization.
It is desirable that as many complaints as possible be handled by the branch. At the same time customers must be able to go further within the institution if they are unhappy with what they hear from the branch to resolve their complaints.

The institutions have all assured me that they will take steps to improve their complaint resolution procedures. Moreover, the enhanced disclosure provisions in our legislation will ensure that customers are informed of these procedures.

Where a complaint has not been resolved by the institution, the Superintendent of Financial Institutions will mediate. Furthermore, he will prepare an annual report to the Minister of Finance to table in Parliament on the number of complaints
June 30, 1988

and their disposition. I have asked that an interim report on this be made available in six months.
In order to ensure that the changes relating to the complaints resolution procedure meet the needs of customers, I have asked the Superintendent to do something further. I have asked him to assess the operation of the over-all system in the country within the banking realm for handling complaints and report to me on the results of this evaluation. The Superintendent is considering engaging the services of a specialist to assist in this evaluation. Not only are we putting a mechanism in place, we are going to monitor it and report back on the monitoring.
In summary, I am seeking a legislative mandate to require better disclosure on the opening of personal accounts and of service charges that may be related to those accounts. Furthermore, that mandate will provide for a clear notification period for increases in service charges.

At the same time, most major deposit-taking institutions will be providing basic banking services at little or no cost. In cases where these institutions have imposed service charges, identified by the committee as unfair, they will be withdrawing them. The complaints procedures within the institutions will be strengthened and I am formalizing the responsibility of the Superintendent for mediating complaints.

Today's measures serve to underline our Government's commitment to ensuring that the Canadian consumer, whose deposits form the foundation of our banking system, is treated fairly, frankly and with respect. These measures underline that.
The problem of bank service charges raised by the committee and by Canadians and acted upon today by the Government have, I believe, been addressed. We as a Government will be vigilant in monitoring compliance and in ensuring that the problems identified have been resolved, and resolved by effective action, not red tape.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that once again, the Government was weak-kneed. The Government caved in to the banks. It didn't even listen to its parliamentary committee. It didn't hear the message sent by members of its own Caucus. It did not even listen to Canadian consumers. It lacked the courage to do so, and that is typical of this Tory Government. It is a Government without a backbone.
Mr. Speaker, anticipating action by the Government, the Hon. Member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan) considered withdrawing his Private Members' Bill on bank service charges, after introducing it with a lot of fanfare.
Statements by Ministers
We were also surprised when the Hon. Member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan) and the Chairman of the Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs voted against their own bill this week in the House.
I hope the Hon. Member will keep his bill in the running- he is here-after reading the totally inadequate measures announced this morning by the Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Hockin).
Mr. Speaker, we saw before us a Minister who lacked courage. The report of the House of Commons Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs concerning bank service charges contained four types of recommendations. First, it recommended that financial institutions offer their customers a certain number of basic services free of charge. Second, it recommended that financial institutions keep their customers better informed of bank service charges. Third, it asked for the appointment of an ombudsman to defend the interests of customers and finally, it recommended a number of penalties in case of non-compliance with the legislation.
Obviously, we agreed with these recommendations and we strongly support such measures.
When the Finance Committee proposed free basic banking services the big banks were hopping mad. The President of the Royal Bank of Canada said that it would "impose unfair and unjustified costs" for all bank customers; that it would "distort pricing, tending to increase substantially other service charges". Those statements are taken from The Globe and Mail of June 9, 1988.
Yet, the banks themselves admit that occasionally they do provide free basic services to some four million senior citizens and young people. Now, apparently, most of them agree with "voluntary" measures to provide basic services free. In today's The Globe and Mail there is an article which states:
But Toronto Dominion representative Sue de Stein vowed that the country's
fifth-largest bank will not budge on what it regards as a question of principle.
The bank intends to stay competitive in customer services but it doesn't want
government dictating how banks run their business, she said.
"We have no intention of giving in on this principle," she added.
So, Mr. Speaker, I am wondering what all the fuss was about. On the one hand the banks oppose free banking services, and on the other hand they claim that they already do provide some such services, and they now agree-if we are to believe them-to provide more. I am not sure if all this outcry was really serious.
I wish to quote what the Finance Committee had to say about voluntary measures: "The committee welcomes any voluntary action on the part of financial institutions to provide basic services, but worries that voluntary provisions on an institution by institution basis will fall short of what is needed". That quotation is from the report.

June 30, 1988
Statements by Ministers
The Liberal Party agrees with that statement and thinks that today's measures put forward by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) are totally inadequate.
In this morning's newspapers one reads that one of the largest banks, the Toronto-Dominion Bank, is still dickering over service charges. I wonder how the Government will oblige the Toronto-Dominion Bank, or any other bank for that matter, that in future will refuse to comply with voluntary measures. How will the Government oblige them to comply with the guidelines? There are no teeth in this morning's measure. There is nothing in there that gives the Government any stick to bring the banks into line with.

Mr. Speaker, the Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs recommended fines or penalties of up to $10,000 for a first offence and up to $100,000 for each subsequent offence committed within a period of three years. There was no mention in the Minister's statement this morning of any serious measures or penalties to force the banks to act.
As far as the ombudsman is concerned, he will be in a very difficult position because his role will not be to arbitrate but to act as a mediator in case of a dispute.
Admittedly, he will have to report to the Minister once a year, and the Minister will have to table a report in the House, but, Mr. Speaker, when a consumer's rights are violated, that person should be able to get some basic justice from the ombudsman; the Government did not accept this recommendation of the Committee.
What will happen, Mr. Speaker, if a conflict between a bank and a customer goes on and on? Who will settle it? We do not know.
Finally, the Minister's statement this morning is not specific on the measures to better inform customers about bank service charges. We do not know if there is a time limit. Will the customers have prior notice? Will there be time limits in the legislation to prevent abuse by the banks?
We in the Official Opposition would like the Government to include time limits in the legislation so that Canadian consumers really receive the services and are fairly treated.

Indeed, in my opinion, there is very little in this statement to satisfy Canadian consumers. It appears that the Minister went to his friends in the banking industry and said: "Hey, I need your support. I need your help. I need your co-operation. We have an election coming up and this could be a very sensitive issue. So, come on, friends, be nice to us, co-operate with us, do it voluntarily and we will be nice to you sometime. For God's sake, fall into line, don't do anything to hurt us now. We are politically involved in a very serious game called an election in Canada this year and we wouldn't want the banks to be embarrassing to the Government".
This is a spineless Minister. This is a Government that has no courage, and it did not do much this morning to improve the image that it has in the country.

Mr. Speaker, having listened to the Minister today and read his statement, my conclusion is that this is the biggest bank hold up since the great train robbery. What the Minister has said today is a crock. It is an absolute cop-out.
Last fall Members in the House raised very serious questions not only about the proliferating bank service charges, but about the ever-increasing charges on services. There are approximately 180 different services in any given bank, and the charges have kept going onward and upward.
As a result, the Standing Committee on Finance investigated. Having heard the witnesses, the committee stated that the complaints of consumers are justified. It recommended several tough recommendations all the way from a no-frill basic bank account, to services for which there is no charge, to an ombudsman, to notification.
We in the New Democratic Party were not satisfied with those recommendations. As far as they went, we said that they were fine, but that they had to be tougher. We wanted an independent, autonomous ombudsman, and we put that recommendation into a minority report. We stated that there ought to be redress for the billions of dollars that the banks have heisted from the pockets of Canadian consumers. We said that there ought to be a freeze on bank service charges starting in the year in which the report was tabled in the House.
Following that report, the Hon. Member for York Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan) entered a Private Member's Bill, which was patterned exactly after the report, complete with regulations. The Chairman of the Bankers Association, Robert Macintosh, went wild. The banks went wild. They said that politicians had tin ears, that the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) was a socialist, and that the only reason the members of the committee recommended those tough things to tell banks what to charge was that they were afraid of their seats. He also stated that there was no such thing as a free lunch, and that no one would ask the supermarkets to give free groceries to people, therefore, he asked, why are the banks asked to provide free services? That was the reaction of the banks.
Now, what has happened? What happened to the Hon. Member for York Scarborough and the Member for Mississauga South? The following is what the Hon. Member for Mississauga South said in debate on Thursday, June 23, as reported in Hansard-.
However, clearly, the kind of arrogance and lack of sensitivity expressed by the President of the Bank of Nova Scotia in his letter and other letters as a result of other actions, leave the Government with very little alternative except to proceed with the legislative hammer and regulatory control. It is important that that regulatory hammer and control be effected properly.
June 30, 1988

Then he went on to say, Mr. Speaker:
I suspect that had the committee report been before the committee today, it
would have been harsher than it is.
Now, what has happened to this roaring rabbit? There has been a conversion. He is nothing but a copy-cat today. Why? Because all the banks except one said, Oh well, we accept voluntary compliance. They said that, not because they honestly believe it. In fact, it is anathema to their very philosophy that the Government should tell them what services to charge for and how they should deliver the services. It is not part of their economic thinking. It is not part of their business philosophy.
So why did the Minister surrender? Why did he accept the fact? I mean, this Minister asking consumers to accept that the banks will voluntarily restrain themselves is like asking the Canadian public to believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) when he says that our social programs are a sacred trust. There is as much veracity to what the banks are saying as to the experience Canadians have had with the Prime Minister's promises.
Hear, hear!
Now, why did the Government do this turnabout? Because, in fact, they are not interested in protecting consumers. In a recent poll carried out by Angus Reid, it showed that 75 per cent-
Who?

I know the Liberals do not like Angus Reid these days. I know he is persona non grata over there. The survey showed that 75 per cent of Canadians believe that the only way to deal with the banks in terms of bank service charges, was by government intervention, by regulation. The Consumers'-
Nationalization.
The Consumers' Association of Canada said that while they will accept this sudden death-bed repentance by the banks, in fact the only effective way is through government legislation.
I thought you were going to nationalize-

Mr. Speaker, I heard the Liberal spokesman speak on this, condemning the Government, but last Thursday the Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) got up and said that she prefers this voluntary compliance, that there was really no need for the Government to legislate.
Where do they get their money from?

I understand that the Liberals have some difficulty with their banking services these days. It may be why the Royal Bank did not contribute anything to them in 1986.
Statements by Ministers
The question has to arise-why? I think it is because this crock of voluntary compliance is in line with Tory philosophy. In fact, they are true to themselves.
Secondly, Canadians are well aware of the fact that the banks contribute considerably to the Conservative Party. As a matter of fact, in 1986, the five banks contributed $177,000 to the Conservative Party. In an election year, that doubles. For example, in the year 1984, they got $360,000 from the banks. This year, given the inflation factor, it will approach $400,000, no doubt about it.
So, do Canadians really expect them to bite the hand that feeds them? Not on your life. The banks have made the argument with the Government: Well, we will regulate ourselves. We will accept certain things. We went through this a little over a year ago. This House, the Finance Committee, did an investigation of bank credit cards because the credit card interest rates were skyrocketing. The Finance Committee did a study. The banks said, "We will voluntarily roll it back", and they voluntarily rolled it back.
I suggest to you, if you went now and looked at the interest rates on bank credit cards you would notice they are moving right back up again to their heights prior to the study.
Canadians do not trust the banks to comply voluntarily. In fact, the Toronto-Dominion Bank has said it will not comply. In an oligopoly, that is what you need, one leader. The Toronto-Dominion Bank will become the bench-mark against which all the other banks will determine their own service charges.
Nationalize them.

Mr. Speaker, the other argument that the banks use and which the Government has accepted is that there is no free lunch. The banks have asked, why should they give free services? Look at what the Canadian taxpayers have given to the banks. This Government, the taxpayers of Canada, allowed them to write off their Third World debt against their Canadian earnings. It is worth about $3 billion. Who picks up the tab when the banks do not pay their fair share of taxes? Ordinary Canadians. They pick it up.
Hear, hear!

Furthermore, we have allowed the banks of this country collectively to defer taxes, which they will never pay. Who pays when they do not pay? The ordinary, average Canadians pay.
As Ernest Hemingway said in The Sun Also Rises: "They will pay and pay and pay". Canadians are sick and tired of paying and paying and paying to keep this Government in the position where it is today.
Watch your ticker!

Now, who is getting the free lunch? The banks are getting the free lunch. The question has to be asked,

June 30, 1988
Committee Reports
after this statement by the Minister: Do things change for Mrs. de Gruchy? Does she have any more assurance, or does any other consumer have any more assurance that when they go to the bank to get quarters, they won't get dinged and donged? No, Mr. Speaker. No assurance.
Would any Canadian from a small business who goes in to get 50 cents in pennies not be charged 40 cents? No. There is no guarantee. There is no assurance that the banks won't ding and dong them again and again and again. Look at what they suggested, with respect to an ombudsman.
Now, there is one office in Ottawa, but surely it stretches the credulity of Canadians even to think that this office protects consumer interest. Do you know what office that is?
Harvey Andre.

It is the office of the Superintendent of Financial Services. Now, if this Government or anybody believes that that Superintendent of Banks really has the interest of consumers at heart, have I got a bridge for them. Have I got a bridge!
Mr. Speaker, the Superintendent of Financial Institutions is only concerned about the solvency of banks. They are not interested in the problems of Mrs. de Gruchy or Go-Go Pizzas or any of the hundreds and hundreds of complaints we have had about bank service charges. Eighty-two per cent in the survey said that what we need is an independent economist ombudsman with the power to advocate and the power to referee. That is what we needed. We do not need to have the office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, with all its little agents running around checking on solvency of banks, to deal with these very important and specific problems that consumers have with banks.
So the New Democratic Party said, that is what is needed. The Tories can laugh and they can make fun of it all they want. They are out of step with what Canadians want, and that is a little bit of justice when they are dealing with these bankers. The banks charge you when you put your money in the bank, they charge you now when you take the money out of the bank. They charge you to keep money in the bank. All of these things will continue. Nothing will change. It is now getting to the point where you walk in the bank and be charged.
One reporter was telling me yesterday that he went to get a print-out of his account, which cost him $3. He told me that about two weeks ago the print-out cost a buck. He was told that this was the new charge system, Mr. Speaker. And that is the Toronto-Dominion Bank. Does this change anything, Mr. Speaker? No. This Government has entered into collusion with the banks to hold up the Canadian public and pick their pockets. Last year the bank picked people's pockets to the tune of $750 million. The bonanza is coming because the Government has shown it is the banks' best friend.
Let me say to the Minister that Canadian consumers and we on this side of the House are deeply disappointed with the statement of the Minister. It is a complete surrender, totally unacceptable to the New Democratic Party and to thousands and millions of Canadians.

subsubtopic: RIGHT TO LIFE OF THE UNBORN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by a number of residents of my constituency of Burnaby who state that the right to life is a paramount and most fundamental right of a person.
They state that the paramount right to life is vested in each human being from the moment of fertilization without regard to age, health or dependency. They state further that the word "person" applies to all human beings irrespective of age, health, functional condition of dependency, including their unborn offspring at every state of their biological development, including fertilization. They call upon Parliament to prepare legislation immediately to the effect that no unborn person shall be deprived of the right to life except where medical procedures are required to prevent the death of the mother.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by a number of residents in my constituency of Burnaby who note that the Conservative Government had no mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a free trade agreement with the United States.
They note that this trade agreement negotiated by the Mulroney Government threatens the very fabric of Canadian, political and economic sovereignty. Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to outline briefly to the House the amendments proposed to the National Housing Act and to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act. The Bill contains provisions which support the Government's ongoing commitment to help house Canadians.
The amendments focus on mortgage loan insurance and mortgage-backed securities, two government programs designed to encourage a continuing flow of investment funds for housing. Other amendments in the Bill are designed to ensure that the mortgage insurance fund operates more effectively and, ultimately, becomes self-sustaining on an actuarial basis.
Incidental amendments are included to clarify wording and to repeal obsolete sections. These amendments comprise part of an ongoing review by this Government to ensure that under the federal housing policy, all Canadians have decent, adequate and affordable shelter.
With mortgage insurance for mobile homes which is also introduced in the Bill, young couples, families, singles and seniors will find financing this type of home far less costly than in the past. By providing mortgage insurance for these economical homes, we are significantly increasing the number of Canadians who can achieve home ownership and build family equity.

June 30, 1988
National Housing Act and CMHC Act
Equally important to home financing, whether private or government assisted, is the amendment designed to use existing mortgages for mortgage-backed securities. The extra millions of dollars of mortgage funds they encourage should continue to result in longer term mortgages at more stable interest rates.
The benefits in reduced monthly payments for fixed terms will truly aid more Canadians to fulfil their dream of home ownership. Furthermore, they will provide all of us, and particularly our growing senior population, with secure government-protected investments.
This Government has been vigorous in encouraging home ownership through sound economic management and government mortgage insurance initiatives. By working with the provinces and by directing all government funds to those most in need, more low-income Canadians, the disabled, women raising families on their own, widows, victims of family violence and young singles have secure, affordable housing. Only recently, co-operative housing groups have received additional support. This has been welcomed by those in the coop housing movement.
The amendments with respect to social housing reaffirm the agreements for provincial contributions to housing for the needy and open the doors to home ownership to thousands more Canadians. I would like to take this opportunity to thank the Members of the House for their support in helping us achieve these goals and for agreeing to deal with this Bill so speedily today.

There have been sentiments expressed in the House by Members on all sides who are seriously concerned about this crisis. I received a letter from a constituent of mine, which I think would be of interest to Hon. Members on all sides of the
House because it expresses probably in a better way than I could the frustrations that are felt by many people in Toronto who can no longer afford to buy homes. My constituent wrote:
My husband is a teacher and I'm an administrative assistant. Though we earn a decent income between us, the current situation makes it unlikely that we'll ever own a home or our own. Though 1 know it has never been possible for everyone to own their own home I think its very sad when even the smallest house is beyond the reach of the average person or family. So that a privileged few can make large amounts of fast money, a huge number of potential homebuyers are put out of the market permanently.
Adding to the hopelessness of the situation is the fact that rents are so high in Toronto that even a small downpayment takes years to save. Generally, by the time one saves the downpayment on an average home, the price of the home (and the required downpayment) has doubled.
I've lived in Toronto all my life and I love it here, but it now appears that if we want to start a family David and I will have to move to a smaller city nearby and hope to gain employment there (unless we want to raise a family in an apartment building).

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (for the Minister of Agriculture) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-141, an Act to regulate the marketing of agricultural products in import, export and interprovincial trade and to provide for national standards and grades of agricultural products, for their inspection and grading, for the registration of establishments and for standards governing establishments, be read the second time and, by unanimous consent, referred to Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, today I would like to speak to the Bill we just tabled which concerns agricultural products in Canada. I may add that speedy passage of this Bill is urgently needed. Mr. Speaker, we need this Bill first of all to clarify and reinforce the role played by the federal Government in the agricultural sector. This legislation will give the federal Government more clear-cut statutory powers to regulate the marketing, inspection and grading of agricultural products and to provide for national standards and grades. It will help improve agricultural trade, both in Canada and on the international market.
Bill C-141 also provides better protection for the Canadian consumer. Speedy passage of this Bill is of the utmost importance to all Canadians, and especially to the agri-food industry. As you know, it is also of vital importance to the Canadian fruit and vegetables industry, whose 27,000 growers of fresh fruits and vegetables now have annual sales of over $1.7 billion. That is impressive, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian Horticultural Council and the Canadian Fruit and Wholesalers Association agree that this legislation is essential to maintaining a well-organized market.
The two groups I just mentioned are among the twenty-seven national agri-food organizations supporting this Bill. At the present time, standards for these products are regulated under the Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act. In fact, very few amendments have been made since the legislation was passed in 1955. As you know, the Act contains a number of shortcomings and ambiguities that were already pointed out some time ago. Some regulations have become practically unenforceable. That is why we must act now to provide the requisite authority to revise the regulations covering agricultural products. For instance, sub-paragraph 7(iii) of Clause 31 of the Bill will again give us the power to control consignment selling of fresh fruits and vegetables.

Until 1983, consignment selling was controlled under the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act of 1935. The Act was amended in 1942 to prohibit imports of produce which the importer purchased later than 24 hours after shipment and from the point of production. This effectively controlled consignment selling.
When the CAPS Act was introduced 33 years ago, it consolidated a number of existing Acts, including the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act. However, the import provisions concerning consignment selling, Sections 56 and 57, were not consolidated but remained under the original Act.
For over 40 years these regulations controlled imports on a consignment basis. In other words, imports could only enter Canada under a prior purchase agreement. However, in January of 1983, the Standing Joint Committee on Regulatory Scrutiny examined the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act. It ruled that the Act did not have the enabling authority to regulate consignment selling.
In more than five years there has been no attempt to enforce such regulations. However, last summer notice was served that Canada's fresh fruit and vegetable markets are vulnerable to surplus products from abroad. These surplus products can be sold at depressed prices in direct competition with Canadian production and pre-purchased imports.

Without controls on consignment selling, Mr. Speaker, products can be imported without a prior purchase agreement. Blemished products can be offered for sale, causing prices to fluctuate in a market that is already unstable.
Controlling consignment selling does not in any way affect our free trade agreement with the United States.
During the talks, we clearly explained our position to the U.S. negotiators. They are well aware that Canada intends to take action in this respect.
In fact, these controls are entirely in line with the rights and obligations we have under GATT.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill also guarantees us some flexibility in cases where it would be undesirable or impractical to apply the present Act.
For example, test marketing of new products or new packaging would be impossible if it were not exempted from the requirements of the Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act. Furthermore, packers and processors of fresh fruits and vegetables must at times be temporarily exempted from the packaging and grading requirements when some Canadian products are in short supply.
Subparagraph 31(1 )(iv) of this Bill authorizes the Minister or his delegate to allow the bulk transport of fruits and vegetables in containers that do not meet the regulatory standards. This makes possible the orderly, efficient interprovincial or international sale of fresh or processed fruits and vegetables when shortages occur on the domestic market.
Section 15 of the Bill authorizes us to make logos and quality names for agricultural products into national brands. Making trade marks of federal quality names will increase the effectiveness and credibility of our inspection system. The
June 30, 1988

resulting constant quality will clearly benefit consumers, Mr. Speaker.
Improved controls on imported products or those sold interprovincially will protect consumers from products that do not meet our health standards.

Additional provisions will allow Agriculture Canada to respond to developments in the agriculture sector and provide authority for cost recovery and privatization. Proposed revisions will increase penalties established in 1955 and provide a general updating of the Act similar to revisions made to the Meat Inspection Act in May, 1985.
To ensure the use of fair and ethical trading practices and the orderly marketing of safe, wholesome agricultural products, it is necessary to improve the licensing of dealers of agricultural products. This is prescribed in Section 32(b). It clearly defines the terms and conditions under which dealers can operate.
This Bill will ensure that the new marketing procedures work fairly for dealers and buyers of fresh fruits and vegetables.
The Canadian Board of Arbitration and the Review Tribunal, which now operate under the Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act, would be maintained. I refer the House to Clause 4 of the Bill. The Board will consider complaints against dealers and provide rulings in accordance with the Act. The tribunal will hear any appeals against the Board's rulings.
The Canada Agricultural Products Act will update current provisions governing trade and product standards. Outdated and impotent legislation will be replaced with legislation that can help guide the agri-food industry into the 21st century.

Better regulations in the farm export industry would certainly enhance Canada's image as a supplier of healthy and high quality foodstuffs.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize the continuing support of our colleagues, especially in the Niagara Peninsula area.

I am thankful for the warm support of the Members for Lincoln (Mrs. Martin), Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson), St. Catherines (Mr. Reid) and Welland (Mr. Pietz) and the surrounding area. Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us today is certainly much broader than we had called for under the Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act. It goes far beyond the simple provisions relating to consignment selling and to bulk shipments.
This issue has been before the Government since at least 1984. It has not been able to enforce the old Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act regulations since 1984. The Canadian Horticultural Council has been calling for action since 1984. Last summer, the entire frozen sour cherry industry was destroyed because the Government refused to act even though it had promised for years to bring in amendments.
I cannot help but have the same feeling today, the last normal sitting day, that I had last year with the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The Government brought in a Bill and allowed for a briefing of opposition Members in the lobby in the last hour before the House sat. We allowed the Bill to go through in one sitting. There were probably many flaws in the Bill because we did not have public hearings. The Government then took eight months to proclaim the Bill.
The Government will demand that this Bill be passed immediately, but will reluctantly proclaim the Bill next January or February, as they did with the Farm Improvement Loans Act. It is not only unreasonable, it is unfair to agriculture and certainly unfair to the House of Commons to bring in legislation in the dying hours of the session. It shows no respect for the House.
We know that the Canadian Horticultural Council needs this legislation and that the cherry producers need the legislation this year. We want to co-operate, but we are opposed to the Government treating the industry and the House of Commons with contempt, as it does year after year. We are faced with the ultimatum to either pass the legislation or let the industry be destroyed without it. The Government is showing utter contempt, as it did last year with the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
The Minister said that this legislation is leading the industry into the 21st century. The joke is that as a result of the free trade agreement that his Government is hammering through this House, the industry will not be around in the 21st century. Much of the industry will be destroyed with the loss of the seasonable tariff.
The grape industry will be destroyed. We learned yesterday that the Government will provide some $35 million in the Ontario region for the grape industry. Yet the grape industry requires at least $156 million just to cover its losses in the adjustment as as result of the trade deal. This industry was sacrificed because the President of the United States tipped his glass of wine with the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES

Mulroney) at Rideau Hall and said that he will not be happy until the entire Canadian grape industry and wine industry is destroyed and Canadians are drinking California wine. Clearly he is getting his wish. If the Government is going to sacrifice the grape and wine industry in Canada, the least it could do is pay some reasonable adjustment.
Furthermore, the Government is demanding that the Ontario Government pay a similar amount when it knows that Ontario has openly and consistently opposed the trade deal. The ones who will suffer are the people in the Niagara region, along with those in the Okanagan.
The Minister said that the Members from the Niagara region gave their warm support to this legislation. They will require more than warm support in order to get re-elected after the trade deal is passed. The trade deal will be absolutely destructive.

Every one of them knows it. The Canadian grape industry faces the loss of half their acreage. Some
11,000	acres will have to be removed but they will only get a quarter of the amount they need for compensation. While the Minister of State for Agriculture (Mr. Blais) states that he has warm support, 1 suspect it is very lukewarm. The meaning of "lukewarm" is "not too hot". The Members from the Niagara area are not too hot on this trade deal because they know they will be destroyed. They know the Government has abandoned them. The industry is demanding $156 million because half their grape-vines will have to be torn out. They are getting exactly $35 million. The Minister announces the best he can do with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is some $35 million when the adjustment required is $156 million. Everyone knows what will happen.
