This trade deal is absolutely devastating. I talked to a producer last weekend who has 800 acres of grape-vines in the Niagara area. He is facing their removal. I said to him that surely there will be some market, and he replied, yes, there will be some market, and do you know what the market will be, Mr. Speaker? The average white hybrid grape producer received something around $600 per tonne during the last three years. In 1989, he must compete with the grapes produced in California. The average price he will be competing with is $347, that is assuming the dollar does not appreciate some more, which is what it is doing practically every day. No wonder these producers are going to be put out of business. If they are selling white hybrid grapes for $600 a tonne on the market and suddenly they have to compete with the prices in southern California, delivered in Canada, with transportation and all the other charges, they are looking at $347. It is little wonder they are very concerned.
The Minister indicates he is going to provide about one quarter of the assistance required. This Government is not only sacrificing this industry but will not pay any compensation. The Prime Minister tips his glass to the President and says: "We are going to sacrifice the Canadian grape and wine industry". Surely he should pay the cost. But he is only putting up one quarter of the money.
We are not very happy with a Bill that does all kinds of things that are way beyond the scope of the original regulations which were ruled ultra vires last year. The old Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act was ruled ultra vires in 1984. The Government stopped enforcing it because of the decision of the Special Joint Committee on Regulations and Statutory Instruments. The industry has simply been in limbo with respect to this consignment selling ever since. So the pressure has been there.
The Parliamentary Secretary and the Minister have promised year after year at the Canadian Horticultural Council's annual meeting that they will bring in amendments. That is great, but why bring them in on the last sitting day of the session? This is an industry that could face horrendous problems. Literally millions of dollars were lost last year when the Government refused to bring in amendments relating to bulk shipments for the sour cherry industry.
This is the kind of Bill that should have proper hearings. It has all kinds of legal ramifications relating to search and seizure and relating to interprovincial trade. The Government talks about giving greater freedom for interprovincial trade. If we are going to have a free trade agreement with the United States, it might be good to have free trade between the provinces. Everyone seems to agree with that although Deputy Ministers of Agriculture have had not had much success so far. This Bill, if you can believe it, Mr. Speaker, actually further controls interprovincial trade.
The people in the Department say if we are going to control international trade, as this Bill proposes to do, we have to control interprovincial trade. That may be necessary under the GATT, but I would feel more comfortable if we had some public hearings and had the Deputy Minister for International Trade before the committee. Perhaps we could hear from some of the provinces. Perhaps Nova Scotia does not like this provision. Perhaps British Columbia does not like the provision with respect to interprovincial trade. But the Bill is brought in on the last afternoon of the regular parliamentary calendar to be swallowed whole. I suppose we could take the attitude that some like it. If the Government is going to screw up the country, let it go ahead and do it. But I do not really think it is discharging our responsibility either as members of the Opposition or as Government back-benchers to leave it to Government control.
This legislation will apparently upgrade many sections with respect to the horticultural industry, very much along the lines of the Meat Inspection Act a few years ago. That is desirable. We had public hearings. We brought in various people from
June 30, 1988

the industry to see how it would work. I would think similar kinds of public hearings would be desirable for this Bill. This is a big country, with about five or six distinct agriculture producing areas, and the impacts are very wide. Clause 4 provides for an arbitration and review panel to handle disputes between shippers and receivers. This is very similar to the existing Act. There may be some minor adjustments there because this whole Bill has been brought in on an emergency basis in the way the Government does most things and the details are not provided for us.
The registration of establishments is provided for. This is similar to the existing Act, but there is a whole new section under Clause 14 which provides for contracting out. Apparently the Government has a policy now of contracting out for laboratory work. That may be desirable. I am not judging it one way or the other, but it seems to me it would have been good to hear from the private sector and from government officials as to what standards would be put in place to ensure that the laboratory standards are just as good in private sector laboratories as they are in government laboratories. We do not know that.
There is a new section, Clause 15, for national trademarks which provides for the products which use that national trademark standard and have not met those standards even though they have not crossed an international boundary. They would be subject to federal inspection. I think that is probably a very good provision. There are a number of arrangements with respect to Clause 19 as to how administrative officers are appointed. It is similar to the existing CAP Act. The inspection provisions are very similar to the existing CAP Act.
There is a new section with respect to search and seizure which is not in the existing Act. I have been told by officials that it is similar to the provisions which were put in the Meat Inspection Act, and it is probably useful, but I would have preferred to hear some testimony by officials with respect to the legal limits which are prescribed. There is also a provision for disposal of seized fruit and vegetables and other commodities. There are dramatic changes in the penalties. They have been raised from $500 to $10,000. That may be appropriate. We do not have testimony to prove that one way or the other.
I do want to deal with the question of consignment selling because that has been a problem with shippers in the United States who have surplus fruit and vegetables. Once they are loaded on the truck and moving, they can easily be rolled across the borders. It is a type of surplus disposal mechanism. For many years we were able to control that. Back in the forties it fell under the regulations of the fruit, honey and vegetable legislation. Those regulations were ruled ultra vires in 1984, and nothing has been done since.
We are glad that the Government is bringing in this amendment to change the CAPs Act. We hope that the Government will not wait for eight or nine months to proclaim
Canada Agricultural Products Act
the Act and to bring in the regulations. If it does the value of it for this year's fruit and vegetable producers will be lost.
We heard stories of shipments of boxes of plums coming into the country last year from California which were selling for $10 a box in California. By the time they reached Montreal in a deteriorated condition, they were down to $2 a box. That totally destroyed the Canadian market for those commodities. Similar things happen year after year with regard to peaches and other perishable commodities. They are simply rolled across the border and thus destroy our markets.
Apparently the same arrangement applies to interprovincial trade under this legislation. I am sure that some shippers and producers will be surprised that these regulations are being put in place. Likewise, I am sure that some provincial Governments will be surprised.
In Clause 32(l)(iv) there is a provision for the control of container shipments coming into the country. It states:
(iv) permitting the Minister or a delegate of the Minister to exempt the marketing of any fresh or processed fruit or vegetable in import or interprovincial trade from any of the requirements of this Act or the regulations where the Minister or delegate considers that it is necessary to do so in order to alleviate a shortage in Canada of the fruit or vegetable or an equivalent fruit or vegetable,
Last year, because this legislation was not put in place a year ago last spring as had been promised, we saw the whole frozen sour cherry industry destroyed as a result of massive shipments coming in from Michigan and other points in the United States. This resulted in millions of dollars of lost production in the fruit and vegetable industry. We hope that the Government will not dally with this legislation this year because it will mean a similar loss.
Under its marketing orders to control price, quality and quantity of any fresh or frozen vegetable, the United States has all these powers. This measure will give our Department of Agriculture a similar type of control, belatedly, after a year or so. Law officers of the Crown advised the Government that the regulations which had been drawn for processed fruit and vegetables a year ago should be brought in to control those shipments. Of course, this legislation will firm up the regulations as they apply to fresh fruit and vegetables, as well as to processed fruit and vegetables.
Consideration of the impact that this measure will have on the trade deal is another aspect of the whole agreement which would have been useful if public hearings had been held. Clearly, in the drafting instructions provided to the United States administration there was a provision put in place by the two congressional committees to authorize the President to negotiate the control of vegetable imports into the United States. Our potato producers in the Maritimes may be looking forward to the American Government negotiating import controls. That sounds rather strange when we consider that the Government has agreed to a free trade agreement with the United States. Yet we see in the drafting instructions a measure for administrative action, not necessarily in the trade

June 30, 1988
Canada Agricultural Products Act
deal itself, but for administrative action to authorize the President to negotiate import controls and their levels. Under its marketing orders the American Government can do that at any stage with any fruit or vegetable.
As far as Canada is concerned, under the agreement as long as these requirements of size of container, quality standards and so on are met then the fruit and vegetables can flow into Canada. It is a very unequal arrangement that arises from the free trade deal. Clearly, assuming that these regulations are not protested at GATT when the Government actually has the courage to proclaim the legislation and to pass the regulations, we will be able to control consignment selling, and the rolling of van-loads of fresh fruits and vegetables often in a deteriorating condition into Canada. Likewise, processed fruits and vegetables in bulk containers can be controlled.
I have already outlined what the impact of the trade deal will be with regard to the fruit and vegetable industry with the removal of the tariff on processed food. The seasonal tariff is replaced by something called a snap-back provision which has absolutely no effect. It is only effective providing the farmer does not increase his acreage. In other words, the industry has to retrench if it is expanding and then that whole snap-back provision does not even operate.
The snap-back provision is a total joke. It provides that if the price drops below 90 per cent of the five-year average, removing the highest and lowest years from that five-year average, then the original most favoured nation tariff can be reinstated. Of course, those prices have to prevail for five days. There is also an administrative period of another two days to consider. I do not know of any fruit or vegetable producer or distributor who believes that once the price of a fresh fruit or vegetable breaks even for 48 hours it can ever be brought back in that season. It may make some people feel better to reinstate the tariff, but it has absolutely zero impact on holding up the price.
Of course, we have the disadvantage of being in a colder climate where many of our perishable fresh fruits and vegetables come on to the market three or four weeks later. Now we will always be taking the lower price at the end of the market.
We have been calling for this legislation to protect fruit and vegetable producers for at least one and a half years. We want to see it passed and have the protection. We are very concerned that the Government will not proclaim it for six or eight months, in the same manner as the Farm Equipment Loan Act. Although we have the worst financial crisis since the 1930s, the Government did not bother proclaiming that Act for six or eight months. We could face a devastating year for fruit and vegetable producers like the sour cherry processed producers faced last year, and the Government will fail either to proclaim the Bill or write the regulations and put them in place. We were assured by officials that those regulations can
be put in place in a week or so. We on this side want to see the legislation passed. We think that the industry is facing a tremendously difficult time with the trade legislation.
In February I had the opportunity to attend the annual meeting of the Canadian Horticultural Council. At that meeting there was a panel on the opportunities for free trade. I listened carefully to all the problems of the various sectors in the industry. I heard practically nothing in terms of opportunities from the trade deal for the fruit and vegetable industry. It is facing an incredibly difficult time.
I have already described what is happening to the grape and wine industry. It will be destroyed. Today I read a confidential document from the American Agriculture Producers Advisory Committee. It is the same as the Canadian SAGITS. They stated that they were quite pleased with the free trade deal, because they felt that right off the top in the grape and wine industry they were going to take at least $60 million of additional wine exports into the Canadian market. When one considers that our wine production is in the area of $210 million that is a pretty significant chunk of the industry.
We believe that if the Government is going to sacrifice the grape and wine industry, as the Prime Minister has decided to do, it should at least pay adequate compensation. We have been told that the compensation will only be $35 million over a six-year period, and the industry is asking for $153 million in the Ontario region alone. It seems like a total disregard for anything that is fair or just for that industry.
The Government has decided to sacrifice that industry and it is not willing to pay the money. The federal Government is saying that the provincial Government should pay the money. Surely the provincial Government through bringing in its legislation relating to the trade deal, whether it is for water, hydro, or medical services, has laid it on the line that it is not supporting the federal Government plan to sell out the industry. Why would the federal Government expect the provincial Government to provide the industrial adjustment for the industry?
Some 17 producers have already been put out of business in Ontario, and more and more are walking away. That is not surprising. If a producer is selling grapes this year at $600 a tonne and as a result of the trade deal that producer will be selling them for $347 a tonne next year, there is no question that the producer will go out of business.
The legislation before the House today will provide some assistance in controlling the imports, assuming that the Government passes it, and assuming that regulations are put in place. The industry is facing a very severe challenge in the future because it is being sacrificed in the free trade deal.
In committee we will look forward to receiving answers to some of the questions that I have raised. I hope the Minister of State for Agriculture will be able to provide those answers. This is a much larger Bill than we had anticipated. It goes far
June 30, 1988

beyond the question of consignment selling and bulk shipments. It is brought forward in the last days of this session. It should have had a much more extensive committee study. We should have heard officials from the whole fruit and vegetable industry, from provincial governments, and from marketing boards in order that we would know what will be the impact of the interprovincial regulations, and the impact with regard to the whole industry from such an extensive Bill that was not envisaged and on which we heard nothing until one day ago.
In fact, we thought the Government had decided not to bring it in. I hope it will not simply be window dressing. If the Bill is not proclaimed and regulations are not drawn almost immediately, we will see many producers destroyed in this very crop year because of the Government's negligence to put in place the proper regulations to control imports from the United States. The Government has known about those problems for almost four years. In October and November, 1984, the Government was told that the regulations for consignment selling under the old Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act were ultra vires. One year ago the Statutory Instruments and Regulations Committee told the Government that the regulations with regard to bulk shipments were illegal, and that they could not be enforced for processed food. They were also told that they were probably ultra vires for fresh fruit as well.
Yet this legislation to give the proper legal framework for those regulations to control those two serious problems for the fruit and vegetable industry were not brought in until this morning. We hope that there will not be more mistakes and errors in it. We hope the Government will act, because it is destroying the industry through the free trade deal. We hope that the Government will at least try to take this one action which can be useful in controlling these abuses which have been going on for several years and have been extremely costly and harmful to agriculture producers in the fruit and vegetable industry.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-141, an Act to regulate the marketing of agricultural products in import, export and interprovincial trade and to provide for national standards and grades of agricultural products, for their inspection and grading, for the registration of establishments and for standards governing establishments.
This particular Bill came about as a result of a ruling or a decision by the committee on Statutory Instruments and Regulations. It ruled that the regulations Canada was using under the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act and the Canadian Agricultural Products Standards Act were ultra vires because those two Acts failed to deal with the marketing of agricultural products. They were simply attempting to designate some of the other rules and regulations as having to do with standards, quality, and grades. The committee of the two Houses of Parliament, the Committee on Statutory Instruments and
Canada Agricultural Products Act
Regulations, found that the scope of powers that the Department of Agriculture was attempting to use lie outside of the scope of the legislation.
This legislation has been promised by the Minister for almost one year. It has been brought before us on the last day of June on a rush basis. The House has agreed to forgo the usual waiting period after introduction, therefore, we have had very little chance to become knowledgeable of the legislation. By agreement, the legislation will go through the House today.
I have had a chance to go through it. I believe I now see why the Minister has delayed so long with the legislation. It approached us before the recess at Christmas, suggesting that perhaps we would have the legislation replacing the CAPs Act at the last day of the sitting at that time. Apparently it was not quite ready and he did not introduce it. We have it now. It is not just a question of chance, on the last day before the July 1 holiday. There are not too many Members in the House. Some of the Conservative Members who represent western ridings have chosen to go home so that they can attend their July 1 functions. As a result, the Minister does not have the problem that I think he would have had had he introduced this when there were more of his own back-benchers around. For the last two decades, at least, the Conservative caucus has refused to allow any agriculture legislation that permits control over the marketing of agricultural products to pass this House, particularly if that marketing involved livestock.
You will know, having been a long observer of this House, that when the legislation to permit the establishment of national marketing boards was established in the early seventies, that a rump of Conservative back-benchers stopped that legislation and in fact made it impossible for even a Liberal Government to bring it in, until they had put in an amendment making it impossible for producers of products to set up a national marketing board for those products, unless the product was named in the legislation.
They totally reversed the intent of the legislation, and it is now necessary to come before the House to have a product named in the legislation before you can begin the slow, tortuous process of setting up a national marketing agency. This House and this Parliament went through that in the case of tobacco. It was one of the first pieces of legislation before us.
Most Members in the House will remember that in spite of that having gone through the House relatively quickly, most of the impetus for the establishment of that national agency had passed by that time. It had taken three years of long, arduous work on the part of tobacco producers, who were going broke and were tired. They never did get their national marketing agency, even though the legislation finally was permitted, three years after it was needed.
What we have is an Act which, by force of the necessities and the exigencies of the way business is carried out, is

June 30, 1988
Canada Agricultural Products Act
permitting and requiring the Minister to have say, legislative and parliamentary say, over the marketing of agricultural products. Which agricultural products does he have the power to control? In marketing, and I quote from the legislation, it means the preparation and advertisement of agricultural products. It includes the conveyance, purchase and sale of agricultural products, and any other act necessary to make agricultural products available for consumption or use.
It is very broad and very necessary for the role that the Department of Agriculture has been carrying on in conjunction with the Horticulture Council of Canada. It goes beyond that because, under this Act, an agricultural product means, (a) an animal, a plant, or an animal or plant product. It is not just plant products, fruit and vegetables or honey that is affected this time. This Act does include animals and animal products. It goes on to say that the agricultural product also means, under (b), "a product including any food or drink, wholly or partly derived from any animal or plant". Or, (c), and this is new, "a product prescribed for the purposes of this Act".
The Minister will have the power under this Act to prescribe other products that do not easily fit within the category of being a plant or an animal product such as, I would presume, honey which comes from a bee and is only indirectly from the plant. What about mushrooms, which by definition are a fungus rather than a plant or an animal?
It gives, I think, the necessary latitude for a Minister of Agriculture to perform his functions and the functions of the Department on behalf of Canadian producers, and I am pleased that this legislation unshackles the Minister of Agriculture in a way that previous legislation did not permit. I am therefore supporting this particular action by the Minister of Agriculture on behalf of the Government.
The legislation also proposes to legalize the arbitration and review tribunal and to give it some enforcement powers, a problem that that particular tribunal ran into under the old Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act and the Canadian Egg Products Standards Act.
A change which I am ambivalent about is that it accredits certain laboratories in the private sector to perform necessary laboratory work. It maintains these laboratories under a system of accreditation, which will be maintained by federal inspectors doing spot checks, by sending some products for testing, to see whether the tests are similar to the ones that have been done by the Department of Agriculture itself. It will, to some extent, be privatizing some of these services that were largely carried out by the Department but can now be shared with the private sector. It establishes an agricultural product legend which has been in use, with the Maple Leaf and the Canada No. 1. It makes this a trademark so that this can be officially used only by the Government of Canada.
I am not sure whether we are going to have some of the spinoff problems with this particular trademark that the Olympic Committee had with the name "Olympic" and the circles and
so on. I would hope not. Otherwise, we may find Air Canada and the Department of Agriculture in court some day, both using the maple leaf. Other corporations, Crown and otherwise, have used the Maple Leaf as well. I think that this makes good sense. The Maple Leaf and the No. 1 are readily identifiable symbols, and I believe that to register that symbol or that legend as a trademark is a necessary part of the marketing of our agricultural products from Canada and within Canada.
This legislation strengthens the rights of inspectors to open containers and it spells out the right of seizure of additional products when an inspection is made by a Department of Agriculture inspector.
Consistent with the new Constitution, the old legislation had to be changed. This legislation is modern in that it specifies there can be no entry to a dwelling or search of a person without a warrant, and the warrants in this case must be issued each day. It is my understanding of this Bill that during the course of such a search under warrant if other illegal products are found, charges can be laid concerning those illegal products even though they were not necessarily specified in the warrant.
Fines have been updated in this legislation because the old legislation had not dealt with the question of fines for 25 to 30 years. We now find that there are two ways of handling the question of fines. Under this Bill there is a procedure for minor offences where the arresting officer or the official of Agriculture Canada can simply issue a fine and ticket the offender for minor infractions and the fine would be paid immediately just as a parking ticket or something like that is paid. Fines for corporations and officers of corporations are now included in this new Bill and those fines will be to a maximum of $10,000 under summary conviction and/or six months imprisonment. Under an indictable offence fines rise to $100,000 and/or one year in prison. Fines have been tightened up considerably, the ability to enforce the legislation and penalties for avoiding the new law are much more onerous than they once were.
Terms and conditions for marketing, importing and exporting in and out of the country and in interprovincial trade will be spelled out under regulations. This is not anything new. Most of this kind of legislation makes the methodology which the Government proposes to follow clearer under regulation. We have had difficulty in previous legislation introduced in a rush by this Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), namely the Farm Improvement Loans Act. That Bill was introduced in a rush last June but was not put into effect until the following February 8 or 10. I have been assured by officials that this Bill comes into effect upon promulgation by the Governor General because there is no clause in it which says the Bill comes into effect upon the proclamation by the Cabinet.
We are allowing this Bill to go through the House quickly on the assumption that it will be in effect within a matter of
June 30, 1988

days. We have been told that the regulations are prepared and that within 10 days or 2 weeks it is hoped to have them published. We are willing from my corner to permit the process to go through quickly. Therefore, I am now prepared for the legislation to move into Committee of the Whole so that the process can be finished in this Chamber.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few minutes to speak on this Bill.
The Government suffers from an acute case of Roy McMurtry syndrome. When I was in the Ontario Legislature, the Attorney General of the province, Roy McMurtry, used to regularly introduce Bills on the last day of the session, expecting passage that very same day. This Government has adopted the same kind of philosophy when it pertains to agricultural legislation. Regularly on the last day of a session the Government brings forward a Bill that it has probably had ready or at least should have had ready for a long time. It wants first reading, second reading, committee stage and third reading on the same day and it expects co-operation from Members of Parliament. Of course, it expects that cooperation having approached Members discreetly beforehand saying that the Government merely wants to correct a portion of a Bill, in this case portions relating to consignment selling and bulk container shipping.
In other words, those two provisions have been turfed out of the old Bill because the regulations were done in a way which went beyond their scope and the Bill was necessary to make that correct. The Minister approached my colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), and told him that. That is partially true, Mr. Speaker. The Bill, in part, addresses those issues, but it goes further. It addresses a number of other important issues.
However, the Bill is not 21st century legislation as the Minister of State for Agriculture (Mr. Blais) stated earlier today. He said, and I paraphrase his words, that this Bill will help to guide the fruit and vegetable industry into the 21st century. But with the free trade deal that his boss, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), has signed there will not be much of a fruit and vegetable industry left in this country at all. The only hope we have is that the Government will be turned out of office before the trade deal and the implementing legislation is over and done with.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext: No chance.
I hear the Member from the Niagara Peninsula across the way. I am sure the grape growers will want to know why the federal Government is offering a mere pittance to the grape growers of that region-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Not true.

-when they will be suffering losses as a result. The Member from the grape growing region of Laval is telling us that that is not true. As an Ontario Member I have
Canada Agricultural Products Act
met the grape growers of our province. He can say that the grape growers do not tell the truth.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No.

He has a right to say that and he can say it all he likes. All the grape growers who are listening will know that they have asked for at least $156 million in reparation for the damage inflicted upon them by the Government as a result of the trade deal. They will be offered somewhere in the order of $30 million or $35 million. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, the federal Government has the nerve to ask the Ontario Government to contribute half of the amount of repairing the damage the federal Government has caused to the Ontario grape growers. That takes nerve. It is the same as if I ran into your car with mine and I asked you for half of the money to fix my own car, Mr. Speaker. That is about the same kind of thinking and it is not surprising given that the thinking comes from the Tory Government.
This Bill goes well beyond the issue of consignment selling, bulk container sales and so on. I want to give an example of some of the things covered in this Bill. It is a very lengthy piece of legislation to be passed in a matter of minutes after a long-winded speech by the Minister of State for Agriculture. Let me read Clause 14 of the Bill:
For the purpose of administering this Act and the regulations, the Minister may designate as an accredited laboratory all or part of any building or place set aside and used for conducting research or carrying out inspections, grading, testing, analyses or experiments in science or used for the manufacture of chemical or biological products.
That goes well beyond the issue of consignment selling and bulk container selling. Clause 13 is even more interesting. It reads:
It shall be a condition of the registration and operation of an establishment as a registered establishment under this Act that this establishment and all agricultural products in it are subject to this Act and the regulations.
What we have here with those two clauses that I have just read is a system whereby the Government can contract or privatize certain services which are done right now by federal government employees.
I have not heard representations from the Public Service Alliance or from anyone else concerning the impact this clause could have on federal government employees. Does the Government intend to use this clause only in cases where there is an emergency and when the technology is already available in the private sector, something which could be deemed to be reasonable, or does it intend to privatize certain services being offered right now by federal government employees? I do not have the answer to that question. It will be very difficult to get the answer to such a question if we are forced to deal with this issue in a matter of minutes.
The Government wants this legislation passed with a few minutes' debate. It is interesting to recall that we dealt with another agricultural Bill earlier this year, the Pedigree Act, an

June 30, 1988
Canada Agricultural Products Act
important Bill. However, I would suggest that the Bill before us today is even more important. The Pedigree Act was discussed for one hour and 31 minutes in the House of Commons and it was debated for three hours and 39 minutes in five committee meetings.
The Bill before us today, which does a number of things which have been described by my colleague from Algoma, by me and by the Hon. Member from the New Democratic Party, is supposed to be dealt with at all stages today without hearing from the provinces, from the industry or from anyone else. We will not even have the weekend to talk to our constituents in order to determine how they feel about this Bill that no one had seen until 11 o'clock this morning.
At 11 o'clock this morning, officials from the Department of Agriculture walked into the opposition lobby, Bill in hand, to brief us while another Bill was being discussed in the House of Commons. There we were sitting in the lobby listening to the debates of the House in one ear and being briefed in the other ear. That is the process the Government wants us to use in order to pass important legislation dealing with agriculture.
As has been said previously, this is the second time the Government has done this.
[ Translation]
At about the same time last year, as the House was preparing to adjourn in late June for the summer recess,-in fact, on the very last day-the Government asked us to adopt another urgent farm bill. It needed it immediately. There were certainly flaws in this bill. We overlooked them. We were not even allowed to hear witnesses because of the so-called urgency. Do you know when the legislation took effect, Mr. Speaker? Eight months later. We had to wait eight months to see this bill implemented. How can we take this Government seriously, Mr. Speaker? I am not saying that we should not take this matter seriously, because it is serious indeed, but I am saying that if this Government was serious, it could have introduced this bill yesterday, the day before yesterday, or even before that to give Parliamentarians at least an opportunity to contact their provincial counterparts and the various farm organizations in this country to seek their support and advice.

The Minister of State for Agriculture talked about the fruit and vegetable industry being guided into the 21st century by this legislation. I do not intend to delay this any longer than I have to, but I must protest with the Minister the manner in which he and his Government have dealt with this issue today, a manner which is disrespectful of this parliamentary institution.
The Government talks about guiding this industry into the 21st century. Let me remind Hon. Members that McCain Foods, earlier this year, wrote to the then Minister for International Trade to tell her in no uncertain terms that the fruit and vegetable industry would be totally devastated by the
actions of this Government. Mr. McLean of McCain Foods can hardly be considered to be someone who is a partisan of my political Party. As a matter of fact, he indicates in his own correspondence that he has been a supporter of the Conservative Party in the past.
Mr. McLean states that he cannot support this kind of legislation because it would totally destroy the Canadian agricultural industry. I have his letter here in front of me. In the interests of time, I will not read it into the record, but I do want to tell Hon. Members that Mr. McLean has indicated very clearly, as a supporter of the Conservative Party and as the representative of the largest food processing company in Canada, that this trade deal is not good for him.
We are talking about leading the fruit and vegetable industry into the 21st century, but we will certainly not be doing that with the Prime Minister's trade deal. That trade deal means total devastation for that industry. The Government knows it. It has chosen to sacrifice the fruit and vegetable industry, the grape growers of the Niagara Peninsula and the Okanagan Valley and several others in the agricultural sector deliberately in order to obtain that trade deal that the Prime Minister wants so badly.
That being said, I will end my remarks by again indicating to the Government that this Roy McMurtry syndrome from which it suffers has to be put out of its misery very soon, and an election should do it.

This being a provincial matter coming under provincial jurisdiction, national trade marks will only be used when they come under national responsibility. On the private and provincial levels, federal jurisdiction will not apply.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES BILL-AMENDMENTS PROPOSED BY CERTAIN CONSERVATIVE MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read with astonishment, not to say disgust, the 136
amendments tabled by the Conservative members who want to sabotage the Official Languages Bill. I think those amendments are bad, racist, and full of hatred.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party of Canada would never have let its members say such divisive remarks. I do not understand, Mr. Speaker, how the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), who himself negotiated the Meech Lake Accord, can keep those members in his Party.
Is the Prime Minister ready to repudiate once and for all those members for their actions and to stop trying to convince Canadians that the Conservative Party is for official languages. When he talks to the French Community, he says he is for, when he talks to the English Community, he says he is against.
Mr. Speaker, could the Prime Minister please make up his mind, it is important for our country!

speakeroldname: Mrs. Shirley Martin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, exactly four years have passed since the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) took over the reins of the Liberal Party, and still they have no defence policy. In fact, searching for the Liberal defence policy is like trying to catch fog in a butterfly net. Not a single original thought has clouded their minds on this vital public issue since 1971 when their last White Paper was tabled.
The NDP, to their credit, have put their few thoughts on paper in the form of a "red" paper on defence. Confused, self-defeating, and ever changing though it may be, the NDP has had the courage to put it forward and face public ridicule. Say what you will about the NDP, they have never been afraid of looking foolish in front of the ordinary people.
The Liberal defence policy, however, seems to be "What we don't know can't hurt us".
If ignorance is bliss, the Liberal caucus must be the happiest group of politicians in Canada. They dither, they ponder, they offer platitudes, but in the end they have no policy and no ideas. They remain as unconvinced and unconvincing as ever. The only defence policy the Liberals have is kept by their Leader to use against his caucus. That, Mr. Speaker, is not good enough for Canadians.
June 30, 1988

subtopic: CALL FOR FEDERAL GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES
CALL FOR FEDERAL GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the riding of St. John's East there is a crying need for assistance for municipal services. The City of St. John's desperately requires sewage treatment facilities to stop the flow of raw sewage into the St. John's Harbour. This will cost about $50 million.
In the Town of Paradise, believe it or not, open ditches are a health hazard because of sewage pollution. The Town of Conception Bay South, the fourth largest community in Newfoundland, needs $55 million now to answer the urgent needs for water and sewage facilities and another $60 million to complete its system.
The Federation of Canadian Municipalities has been Fighting for years to get the Conservative Government to contribute to an aid program for Canadian cities and towns. We in the New Democratic caucus support their proposal and believe the federal Government's one-third contribution ought to be in the form of grants to municipalities. The Federation of Municipalities has shown the economic viability of such a program and the returns to the economy.
Why is the Conservative Government turning its back on Canadian cities and towns? I call on it now to provide the communities of Canada with the help they so desperately need.

subtopic: HOUSING OF YOUNG ONTARIO PSYCHIATRIC PATIENTS IN SENIORS' BUILDINGS
HOUSING OF YOUNG ONTARIO PSYCHIATRIC PATIENTS IN SENIORS' BUILDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many seniors in my riding of London East have expressed concern about the fact that the Ontario Government is now housing young psychiatric patients released from hospital, as well as disabled and handicapped young people, in apartment buildings which were originally designated for seniors only.
It is important that we meet the needs of these young people, but many of the seniors have expressed concern about excessive noise from rock music and late night parties, as well as theft and violence.
I ask the Minister of State for Seniors (Mr. Hees) to raise this matter with his provincial counterparts in the Peterson Government who are responsible for management of these buildings. I believe that this matter should be resolved as quickly as possible.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT BILL C-72 BE PASSED
REQUEST THAT BILL C-72 BE PASSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 30, 1988, the French-speaking people of Canada cannot but be disappointed, especially the ones from Quebec like me, who fought in the last referendum to stay in Canada.
When we see on the Order Paper of the Canadian Parliament, where we have fought for equality of both official languages, motions by 25 Conservative Members proposing that, in case of doubt, the English language shall have precedence over the French language .. .
They go so far as to ask that the language of work in the National Capital, where my collegues from Ottawa-Vanier and elsewhere have fought for years so that the Frenchspeaking Quebec side would get its fair share, should be English only ... And these people have the nerve and the lack of courage ... knowing the attachment the people of Quebec have for Bill 101, to ask that the federal Act take precedence over Bill 101, Mr. Speaker.
Let's hope that the new Mr. Clean from Lac-Saint-Jean will show his mettle and will bring these 25 Members in line. And let's hope that the Prime Minister will stop doing somersaults and invoke closure so that we can pass Bill C-72, the Official Languages Act, and get these stubborn Conservatives off our backs.

Mr. Speaker, in the international arms bazaar just who are the super salesmen?
Perestroika notwithstanding, the U.S.S.R. comes in first by a wide margin with annual arms exports of $120 billion. Yankee traders manage only a little less than half of this. France, with its Mirage jets and Exocet missiles, comes in third at $30 billion.
The prize for most improved performance goes to China, at $11 billion, which has now cornered some 80 per cent of the lucrative Iraq-Iran market.
These countries must certainly be very proud of their contribution to world peace.

June 30, 1988

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-JOHNNY CANUCK CRUSADE
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-JOHNNY CANUCK CRUSADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1911 Oliver J. Wilcox, Member of Parliament for North Essex, was one of the Conservatives who defeated the Laurier Liberals on the issue of free trade. Today his great-grandson, John Wilcox of Salt Spring Island, fights to save Canada from the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal.
On April Fool's Day, a significant date, Mr. Wilcox assumed the identity of Johnny Canuck, the mythical Canadian hero who appears whenever Canada is threatened. Starting from Mile 0 of the Trans-Canada Highway at Victoria, Johnny Canuck drove his rebuilt 1941 Maple Leaf Chevy halfton truck across Canada to warn Canadians about the loss of sovereignty if the trade deal goes through.
Johnny Canuck will be in Ottawa tomorrow to celebrate Canada Day. We welcome Johnny Canuck to our nation's capital and, with millions of Canadians from coast to coast, we join with him in the struggle to keep Canada "the true North, strong and free".

subtopic: MEASURES URGED TO OVERCOME SHORTAGE IN TORONTO
MEASURES URGED TO OVERCOME SHORTAGE IN TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the International Year for the Homeless it is disturbing to learn from an Ontario government report that 200,000 families in the province lack appropriate housing. Unfortunately, this is not news to those living on the streets, in emergency shelters, and those in sub-standard accommodation.
The escalating problem of unattainable housing for the poor, coupled with unaffordable housing for the working middle-class families in Metro Toronto, cries out for immediate federal leadership and co-operation with the municipal and provincial levels of government.
The federal Downsview Airport base, vacant postal lands, and surplus federal properties should be made available for home construction at once. As well, a first homebuyers program, and action on speculative transactions which grossly inflate the prices of homes, should be initiated in order to encourage the availability of reasonable homes at reasonable prices.
The federal Government has ignored this dangerous housing crisis for far too long. It is now time that the Conservative administration exercise its responsibilities if we are to avoid turning the dream of owning a home in Metro Toronto into an ugly nightmare.

Mr. Speaker, today the Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) will be celebrating the fourth anniversary of that fateful day when he became Prime Minister. We all know what the Canadian people thought of that idea.
One item not to celebrate today, however, is his defence policy because he has yet to offer one. We can only look to the sorry past of former Liberal Governments, and the Liberal defence record can be summarized in three words: shame, shame, and shame!
The right hon. gentleman's defence policy remains one of our nation's best kept secrets. He opposed Cruise missile testing because his own caucus was planning to use the Cruise on their Leader if he did not toe the line. He opposed nuclear powered submarines, presumably to uphold the Liberal tradition of rust-out of our navy. But what do the Liberals favour for our defence?
June 30, 1988

It is perhaps most telling to observe the actions of his loyal friend and defence spokesman, the Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith). That Hon. Member, in the next election, has decided that the best defence is to be on the fence, choosing the life of paid lobbyist over explaining the unknown, his Leader's defence policy.
When voting Canadians concerned with our sovereignty ask what is the Liberal policy in the next election, the answer is clear: more of the same, more of nothing, more shame.

Mr. Speaker, 136 amendments were introduced today which should put the Conservative Party to shame.
Those documents reveal the true nature of the beast and make us realize that the Conservative Party has remained antiFrench. I hope that the Prime Minister will be as courageous as his predecessor, Mr. Stanfield, when he got rid of the Hon. Member for Moncton. I think that some of the amendments introduced go against the letter and the spirit of what the Prime Minister himself is spreading across the country. They go against the basic principles, if any, on which the Prime Minister got elected and against his perception of Canadian society and I consider them unacceptable.
Therefore, it remains to be seen if the Prime Minister will intervene to make his party recognize the Canadian duality over the precedence of the English language in Canada. Failing to do so would be unacceptable to all French Canadians. I hope that Conservative Members such as the Hon. Member for Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce) will rise and ask those involved to withdraw from their caucus because their views are unacceptable in Canadian society.

Mr. Speaker, the Economic Summit has come and gone, leaving behind a number of pluses and credits.
The first is to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for his leadership and direction resulting in a successful summit conclusion.
The assembled G-7 leaders tackled many different social and economic problems. Realistic solutions were sought and practical plans were developed.
A big plus must also go to the summit food and drink organizers. Ten years ago, indeed five years ago, no thought would have been given to serving Canadian wines at such an international dinner. But this week was Toronto's week, Toronto's summit. Instead of the usual imports, Canadian wines complemented the summit menu, and were presented with pride and confidence.
Salute to the government advisers, the leaders and their spouses for their support of the Canadian wine industry.
Salute to the Canadian wine industry, the wines and wineries which have, at last, received the reputation that they so well deserve.

subtopic: WAGE GAP BETWEEN MALE AND FEMALE PUBLIC SERVANTS
WAGE GAP BETWEEN MALE AND FEMALE PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday we heard the Government mislead the House by stating that the Employment Equity Act is working to bring equality to the Public Service and in companies under federal jurisdiction. Today we learn that the wage gap between men and women federal public servants actually is widening.
In 1987 the average male public servant made $9,300 more than his female counterpart, an increased wage gap of almost $3,000 since 1981. Why the persistence of this wage gap? Not only are the few women in high level administrative jobs paid less than their male colleagues, female public servants continue to be ghettoized in clerical support jobs, jobs which are low paying and offer few opportunities for advancement.
Canadian women deserve employment equity legislation that works, legislation that applies to all levels of the Public Service, and that includes mandatory pay equity.

Mr. Speaker, the world community is concerned about a thinning of the ozone layer and its consequential effects on all forms of life. Environment Canada is monitoring its status and conducting research relating to the chemical processes in the stratosphere, with investigations to confirm the presence of an ozone hole in the Arctic region, in co-operation with other countries.

June 30, 1988
Oral Questions
The Department has been operating ground based ozone observing stations since 1957. It has developed a modern ozone measuring instrument which has been exported to over 10 countries in recent years. Also, since the late 1950's, Environment Canada has operated the World Ozone Data Centre for the World Meteorological Organization which provides data for scientists on an international basis.
In September, 1987, Canada signed an international agreement, the Montreal Protocol, along with 24 other countries, to control substances that deplete the ozone layer.
Canada is working with its international partners to address this crucial issue, which has to be a fundamental priority for all of us in the global community.

subtopic: SOUTH MORESBY-NEED FOR AGREEMENT WITH HAIDA PEOPLE
SOUTH MORESBY-NEED FOR AGREEMENT WITH HAIDA PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the prospects of a successful agreement on South Moresby grow dimmer. Despite a unanimously recorded vote of this Parliament, the Prime Minister's Office has chosen deliberately to ignore that resolution of May 14, 1987.
A Memorandum of Understanding was reached between Canada and British Columbia last July at a cost of $106 million. Consultations have been pursued in good faith between the Council of the Haida Nation and Crown Canada as represented by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan). Sadly, these have led nowhere and this is confirmed by the Prime Minister's Office this week insofar as those discussions were and are limited to the context of the National Parks Act only.
I believe that Section 35 of Canada's Constitution means what it says. The rights of the Haida in South Moresby are recognized and affirmed. I believe a unanimous vote of this Parliament means what it says, that the Haida be involved in matters affecting South Moresby. I believe that a consent agreement can and must be reached with the Haida Nation and be further negotiated through a framework agreement.
South Moresby will be preserved forever as a direct result of the will of the Haida people and their supporters across Canada. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) should recognize and affirm reality through a Canada-Haida agreement. The Haida people, Canada, and South Moresby deserve respect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday June 9 last, an escape took place, shots were fired and hostages were taken in my riding as three dangerous convicts escaped from the Saint-Vincent de Paul maximum security detention center in Laval.
During this multiple escape, two hostages were taken, a corrections officer and a resident of my riding, Mrs Georgette Richard, who was fortunately released on the same day as a result of a well thought out operation by the Quebec Provincial Police. The three escapees were captured 90 hours later.
1 am shocked and astounded to find out that victims such as Mrs. Richard, a law abiding citizen, received no form of help whatsoever. Indeed, prisoners are better treated than victims. The prisoner who was wounded during the incident was taken immediately to hospital and cared for without having to stand in line. When our victim, Mrs. Richard, whose car was used for the escape and later declared a total loss, asked for a means of transportation to IVAC, an aid agency for victims of criminal violence, some 46 kilometers from her home, the only answer she got was that she should take the bus to get there.
Mr. Speaker, it is crucial that we correct these and other criticized flaws in the administration of justice and that victims be afforded adequate humanitarian, medical and financial support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a question to the Minister of State for Science and Technology. Two and a half years ago Massey Ferguson, now the Varity Corporation, was bailed out by this Government through Massey Combines being spun off and a debt of $207 million being lost to Varity Corporation as a result. Now with Massey Combines bankrupt, Varity in the United States is buying back the conventional combine technology.
1 want to ask the Minister if, to express concern about keeping this technology in Canada, his Government will act to see to it that this combines technology is kept in this country in production for Brantford workers so that there is a future for them and their company.

speakeroldname: Hon. Frank Oberle (Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
subtopic: MASSEY COMBINES-REQUEST FOR RETENTION OF TECHNOLOGY IN CANADA

The first of course is for the workers of the Brantford facility. The second is for the farmers who require parts and tooling for the existing equipment, and finally there is the concern about the technology.
